tagline: Queue batch image-generation jobs locally with ComfyUI — no real-time preview-as-you-draw loop.
verdictSummary: A local ComfyUI job queue with a prompt library and searchable output history reproduces the batch-generation half of Krea reasonably well as a one-sitting build. What it explicitly cannot reproduce is Krea's actual signature feature: a real-time diffusion loop that updates the image live as you draw or adjust a prompt, which needs a specialized low-latency inference pipeline no standard local ComfyUI setup provides.
coreLoopDIY: Write a prompt with generation parameters, submit it as a batch job to a local ComfyUI instance, save every output with its exact parameters for reproducibility, and browse results in a searchable contact sheet — one submit-and-wait cycle per image, not a live preview.
whatYouLose: real-time generation that updates the image live as you draw or adjust settings
a specialized low-latency inference pipeline built specifically for that live loop
hosted GPU capacity, so batch jobs don't queue behind your own hardware
a licensed, curated training dataset behind the model
video generation alongside image generation in the same interface
whyPeopleStillPay: People pay for Krea because the live, draw-and-see-it-update loop needs an inference pipeline engineered specifically for low latency at every keystroke — that's genuinely different infrastructure from a standard batch-oriented ComfyUI setup, not just a faster GPU. The subscription buys that real-time engineering, not the underlying model itself.
prompt:
Build a local batch image-generation manager: a prompt library and job queue in front of a self-hosted ComfyUI instance. Stack: Python, FastAPI, ComfyUI as the local generation backend, a small React frontend. Do not attempt real-time generation — a submit-and-wait batch loop is the honest, buildable scope here.

Core loop: the user writes a prompt with a negative prompt, seed, dimensions, and a chosen ComfyUI workflow, and submits it to a local job queue that runs against the ComfyUI server one job at a time (or a few in parallel if the GPU has the memory). Every completed output is saved with a sidecar JSON recording its exact generation parameters, so any result can be regenerated identically. A searchable contact sheet supports favoriting, tagging, and quick re-runs with tweaked parameters — the closest approximation to iteration this architecture allows, a few seconds to a minute per attempt rather than instant feedback.

This needs ComfyUI installed and running locally with a capable GPU, or pointed at a rented remote GPU box. No cloud API key is required if the user supplies their own model files with an appropriate license.

Do not build: a real-time, low-latency generation loop (this needs specialized inference engineering — streaming diffusion, aggressive step reduction — well beyond wiring up standard ComfyUI, and claiming otherwise would be dishonest about what this architecture can do), video generation, or a hosted service for others to use. State plainly in the README that iteration here means resubmitting a job and waiting, not watching an image update live.

faq.q: Can I import my existing Krea projects?
faq.a: No — Krea's project and generation history live on their servers and aren't exportable in a form this build can read. You'd start a fresh prompt library from your first local batch run.

faq.q: Will it work on my phone?
faq.a: Only as a client to a machine running ComfyUI elsewhere — the generation itself needs a GPU, so you're queuing and browsing jobs from a phone, not rendering on it.

faq.q: What does it cost to run?
faq.a: Nothing per generation if you own the GPU, aside from electricity. A rented cloud GPU instead runs roughly $0.50–$2 per hour, billed only while a job is actually processing.

faq.q: What's the one thing that doesn't survive the rebuild?
faq.a: The live loop itself. Krea's actual product is watching the image change in real time as you draw or type — that immediate feedback is what makes iteration fast; here, every change means resubmitting a job and waiting for it to finish, which changes how you'd actually work with it.
